A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable 31-page versions of CodeHacker. Their text, equations, displays and Appendices A–L support reliable comparison, including matching content relocated by pagination changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, hacking success rates, ablations and reinforcement-learning results in Tables 1–5 and Appendix G, alongside case studies.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results, including the detailed LiveCodeBench results in Appendix G and the case studies in Appendices I–K.

M1.justification: The calibration algorithms, Code Analyst, three generation strategies and appendix prompts remain unchanged. v2 deletes the description of LLM-first generation with stress testing as fallback, but specifies no replacement procedure; this establishes reduced documentation rather than an implemented method change.

E1.justification: Both evaluate the same competitive-programming coverage: 2,000 problems divided equally between traditional and special judges, C++ submissions, and 287 AtCoder problems from LiveCodeBench. The added discussion of repository-level applications introduces no evaluated task.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains CodeContests, HardTests, TACO and CodeContest+ as comparators. Tables 2–3 retain the same model sets, and the RL comparisons are unchanged. Newly cited works do not participate as experimental baselines.

E3.justification: The reported evaluation samples, validator/checker controls, metrics, generation temperature and RL configuration are unchanged. Appendices C–F retain the compiler settings, training hyperparameters and source-based separation of training and evaluation data.

E4.justification: The component ablation and dataset-enhancement analysis in Tables 4–5 retain the same evidence. Appendices I–K preserve the checker, validator, number-theory and construction case studies; no evaluated robustness or sensitivity study is added or removed.

E5.justification: Neither version adds empirical confidence intervals, significance tests or repeated-run reporting. The time-based random-seed initialization instructions for stress generation in Appendix L are identical.

E6.justification: Tables 1–5 and 9 and Figure 2 retain their numerical results and rankings. However, v2 removes the qualitative observation in Section 3.4.2 that a test generated for one submission frequently also breaks other submissions for the same problem.

T1.justification: The problem formulation and hack-success definitions in Section 3.1, metric definitions in Appendix E, and lattice and birthday-attack derivations in Appendix H are unchanged.

C1.justification: The main claims about calibrated adversarial testing, CodeHackerBench, evaluation reliability and RL benefits remain the same. The conclusion's added repository-level wording elaborates v1's existing proposed transfer to SWE-bench and broader software engineering.

C2.justification: v2 removes the explanation that cascading generation improves efficiency and that tests transfer across submissions because human and LLM solutions share logical pitfalls. The main experimental interpretations and the Limitations section remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository pointer in the abstract, absent from v1. It also removes the explicit LLM-first/stress-fallback execution description. Compiler details, RL hyperparameters, hardware information and appendix prompts are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds four references concerning VulAgent, TRACE, repository-level code reasoning and SWE-AGILE, with brief contextual additions in the introduction, related work and conclusion. The Cao et al. year and author update concerns an already cited work.

P1.justification: There are localized edits to the abstract, introduction, related work and conclusion, plus deletion of the cascading/generalization paragraph. Author order and the corresponding-author designation change. The overall section and appendix organization remains intact.

P2.justification: Text reflow relocates existing displays: Table 5 changes columns, Tables 7–8 move from page 14 to page 15, and Figure 3 moves from page 17 to page 18. Display content and design remain unchanged; pages 19–31 are visually identical.

improvement.justification: v2 adds a useful code-access pointer and broader research context, but removes the only explicit LLM-first/stress-fallback scheduling description and its test-reuse explanation. The empirical evidence and technical appendices otherwise remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether the access addition compensates for the reduced procedural documentation, leaving the net quality direction uncertain.
